planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in warm weather into a loose, low-nutrient mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss and perlite or fine orchid bark; keep it constantly moist with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide steady warmth day and night rather than a cool-night drop.

directions: This wide-ranging lowland Southeast Asian species colonizes disturbed, sunny ground from Malaysia to Borneo and Sumatra, making it one of the toughest and fastest-growing pitcher plants for a warm windowsill, terrarium, or greenhouse. Its narrow, urn-shaped pitchers hide a slick, waxy zone just inside the rim rather than relying on digestive fluid alone, causing visiting insects to lose their footing and slide into the trap below. Unlike cool-growing highland Nepenthes, it thrives on constant lowland warmth without a night-time temperature drop, so it makes a good next step for growers moving beyond the easy N. x ventrata hybrid. Pot it in a loose, nutrient-poor mix of sphagnum and perlite or bark, watering only with distilled or rainwater and never fertilizing the soil directly.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts into a loose mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite, and give the plant a vertical pole, trellis, or bark slab to climb; it clasps its leaf bases around a support rather than gripping with a tendril alone.

directions: Native to the mountains and lowland forests of Borneo, this species is prized among collectors for its broad, flattened, boldly ribbed peristome, which in some wild-collected forms nearly closes over the pitcher mouth like an armored lip. It climbs unusually for a Nepenthes, wrapping the widened base of each leaf directly around a tree trunk or mount instead of relying purely on a coiling tendril, so it does best given something vertical to grip in a bright, humid greenhouse or large terrarium. It tolerates a somewhat wider day-to-night temperature range than pure highland species but still needs consistently high humidity and mineral-free water. Feed sparingly and only into mature pitchers rather than fertilizing the growing medium.

planting.note: Pot up nursery starts into a loose, well-draining mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss, perlite, and orchid bark, sized generously since this species eventually forms large pitchers and a sprawling vine; keep constantly moist with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide steady lowland warmth.

directions: This Borneo peat-swamp giant is named for the pair of long, curved, fang-like nectar spurs that hang from the underside of its lid directly over the pitcher opening, likely causing visiting insects to lose their grip on the slick rim below and fall in. Its hollow, swollen tendrils typically house a colony of symbiotic ants that defend the plant from herbivores and enrich the pitcher fluid with their waste, and its pitchers are among the largest and most heavily built of any Nepenthes species. Give it constant warm, humid lowland conditions, bright filtered light, and a sizable, well-draining container, since mature vines can eventually sprawl several feet and produce pitchers big enough to hold a substantial volume of water. Water only with pure rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water and never fertilize the growing medium.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts into a loose, low-nutrient mix of sphagnum moss and perlite or fine orchid bark; keep constantly moist with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide warm, humid lowland conditions year-round.

directions: Widespread across lowland Southeast Asia, this species is easy to identify by the narrow band of dense white hairs just below its peristome, an unusual lure that specifically attracts termites, which feed on the trichomes and are then knocked into the digestive fluid below in one of the more specialized prey-capture strategies among pitcher plants. It is a fast, undemanding lowland grower well suited to a warm, humid terrarium, greenhouse, or bright bathroom window, tolerating a wider range of light and temperature than fussier highland species. Pot it in a loose, nutrient-poor mix of sphagnum moss and perlite or bark, watering only with distilled or rainwater and skipping fertilizer in the soil entirely.

planting.note: Set transplants or divisions into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; this deep-red cultivar is grown identically to the species and needs no winter dormancy.

directions: This selected form of Cape sundew colors up a much deeper wine-red than the typical green-and-red species, especially under strong light, with the same long, strap-shaped, dew-covered leaves that curl slowly around trapped gnats and fruit flies. Like the species, it self-sows readily under good conditions and blooms with small pink flowers held well above the sticky foliage. Grow it in bright light in a constantly moist mix of peat and perlite or pure sphagnum moss, watering only with rain or distilled water, since tap water minerals and soil fertilizer will damage it. It needs no winter dormancy and makes an easy, colorful year-round houseplant or windowsill subject outside its hardiness range.

planting.note: Press small pieces of rhizome or existing sod onto the surface of a wet, sandy peat mix; keep the tray constantly saturated to boggy and never let it dry out, since this Brazilian terrestrial species has unusually large leaves for the genus and correspondingly high water needs.

directions: Native to wet, sandy ground in Brazil, this terrestrial bladderwort is grown for its unusually broad, upright, spatula-shaped leaves, which dwarf the thread-fine foliage of most other Utricularia species, and for its tall spikes of showy violet flowers with a bright yellow-throated lower lip. Like all bladderworts it captures microscopic soil organisms with tiny underground bladder traps rather than visible leaf structures, so the real ornamental appeal lies in the foliage and near-continuous bloom. Grow it in shallow trays of wet, sandy peat mix under bright indirect light or fluorescent grow lights, watering only with rain or distilled water, and it will spread by rhizome to fill a pot within a season. It is frost-tender and best kept as a windowsill, terrarium, or greenhouse subject outside zones 10 to 11.

planting.note: Tuck small plantlets or rhizome sections into the water-holding leaf axils of a live tank bromeliad, or into wet sphagnum moss in a humid terrarium; mimic its native habit of rooting inside standing water rather than ordinary bog soil.

directions: This unusual epiphytic bladderwort grows wild only inside the water-filled leaf tanks of large bromeliads in Brazil's coastal Serra do Mar mountains, producing small, round, floating lily-pad-like leaves on the water surface and striking lavender flowers on tall stalks. In cultivation it is typically grown mounted in a live tank bromeliad kept in a humid greenhouse or terrarium, or in a pot of pure wet sphagnum moss standing in rain or distilled water, since it has no tolerance for mineral buildup or drying out. Like other bladderworts it feeds using microscopic underground bladder traps rather than visible leaf structures, so its main appeal is the curious floating foliage and showy bloom. It is considered a specialist's plant best suited to experienced carnivorous plant growers with stable warm, humid conditions.

planting.note: Sow smoke-treated or scarified seed onto a sandy, nutrient-poor peat mix kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water in full sun; unlike its annual relative B. liniflora, this Western Australian species is a true perennial that dies back to a tuberous rootstock during its dry summer dormancy.

directions: Larger and longer-lived than the more commonly grown annual rainbow plant, this Western Australian perennial produces wiry, upright, blue-green leaves densely coated in glistening sticky mucilage that traps small flying insects and catches sunlight in tiny rainbow flashes, the trait that gives the genus its common name. Showy violet flowers with a cluster of dark stamens appear atop the stems through the winter and spring growing season. It requires a distinct dry, dormant summer rest as a swollen underground tuber, followed by a wet, sunny growing season, making it noticeably trickier to keep long-term than the self-seeding annual B. liniflora. Grow it in a lean, sandy, peat-based mix kept wet only during active growth, watering with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water and allowing the pot to dry out during summer dormancy.

planting.note: Sow smoke-treated seed on a lean, sandy, well-drained fynbos-style mix of sand and peat kept lightly moist rather than boggy; this South African shrub dislikes the constant standing water many other carnivorous plants require.

directions: A woody, resin-covered shrub from the fynbos of South Africa's Western Cape, this plant is technically protocarnivorous rather than fully carnivorous: its narrow, needle-like leaves are coated in sticky resin that traps insects, but the plant lacks its own digestive enzymes and instead relies on symbiotic assassin bugs that live on the plant, feed on the trapped prey, and fertilize it with their droppings. Unlike most carnivorous plants, it wants a lean, sandy, sharply drained soil that dries somewhat between waterings rather than the constantly boggy conditions Sarracenia or Drosera demand, more closely mimicking its native winter-wet, summer-dry fynbos habitat. Star-shaped pink to red flowers appear on mature plants, which can eventually grow into a substantial woody shrub over several years. It is considered a specialist's plant grown mainly by experienced carnivorous plant collectors rather than a typical beginner subject.
